common_name: Midnight Mexican Bush Sage (All-Purple Velvety Fall Salvia)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Midnight bears solid deep-purple flowers and calyxes rather than the bicolor purple-and-white spikes typical of the straight species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Midnight is a selection of Mexican bush sage bred for flowers that are entirely deep purple, both the velvety calyx and the small true flower within it, rather than the purple-calyx-with-white-flower combination typical of the species and of selections like Santa Barbara. The result is a richer, more uniformly saturated purple spike that many gardeners find more dramatic for fall color and cutting. It produces the same long, arching flower spikes from late summer through fall as other Mexican bush sage selections, drawing bees and hummingbirds heavily during a season when many other perennials are winding down. Cut back to about 12 inches after the first hard freeze knocks the top growth back; the plant regrows vigorously from its woody base the following spring. Extremely drought-tolerant and low-maintenance once established.

common_name: Pardon My Pink Bee Balm (Compact Rose-Pink Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Pardon My Pink is a sibling of Pardon My Cerise and Pardon My Purple, sharing the same compact size and improved mildew resistance.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Pardon My Pink bears soft rose-pink, shaggy tubular flowers on a compact eighteen-inch plant, considerably shorter than heirloom bee balm and bred with better-than-average resistance to the powdery mildew that commonly disfigures taller Monarda varieties in humid summer weather. Its flowers draw hummingbirds and butterflies through the summer, and its soft color works as a gentler companion to the more saturated Pardon My Cerise and Pardon My Purple in a mixed planting. Give it good air circulation with adequate spacing to further reduce mildew pressure, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and flowering.

common_name: Petite Delight Bee Balm (Compact Lavender-Pink Mildew-Resistant Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Petite Delight is a long-established compact hybrid bee balm bred for a tidy clumping habit rather than the aggressive spreading of many Monarda didyma selections.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Petite Delight bears lavender-pink, shaggy tubular flowers on a compact plant that stays under 18 inches and, unlike many bee balm cultivars, clumps rather than spreading aggressively by runners, making it easier to keep in bounds in a mixed border. It shows good resistance to the powdery mildew that plagues many older Monarda selections in humid summer weather, and its aromatic, mint-scented foliage and nectar-rich flowers draw hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies through the summer bloom season. Provide good air circulation to further reduce mildew risk, and divide the clump every few years in spring if flowering starts to decline.

common_name: Grand Marshall Bee Balm (Tall Deep Magenta-Purple Mildew-Resistant Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Grand Marshall grows taller than most compact modern bee balm hybrids, useful for the middle or back of a border, and shows notably good powdery mildew resistance.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Grand Marshall bears large, deep magenta-purple, shaggy tubular flower heads on a taller plant than most modern compact bee balm hybrids, giving it more presence in the middle or back of a perennial border while still showing markedly better resistance to powdery mildew than older heirloom bee balm types. Its rich color and generous flower size make it a strong nectar source for hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies through the summer bloom season, and the aromatic foliage is characteristic of the mint family. Provide good air circulation with adequate spacing to keep mildew pressure low, and divide the clump every few years in early spring to maintain vigor and control spread.
